source.title: The Persian Rug: solving toy models of superposition using large-scale symmetries
source.authors: Aditya Cowsik; Kfir Dolev; Alex Infanger

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses superposition and analyzes a sparse autoencoder toy model, but does not measure whether individual neurons respond to unrelated inputs or test any other version of the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results about reconstruction loss, weight statistics, and a toy model's decoding algorithm. These do not measure individual-neuron polysemanticity, so they do not test V1–V7. The paper's citations to other work are not recorded as findings.
record.test_reason: The paper analyses the Elhage et al. toy autoencoder: its weight statistics, reconstruction loss and loss bounds. It never measures whether individual neurons respond to unrelated features, how many do, or what causes it. Superposition appears only as framing in the introduction and footnote 1, a pigeonhole argument rather than a measurement. No version V1–V7 is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors add three points: trained models implement the optimal statistically symmetric algorithm, since their loss matches the Persian rug model; ReLU is near-optimal among elementwise or filtering decoders, up to a constant factor; and new sparse-autoencoder architectures are needed to estimate feature magnitudes precisely.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the Elhage et al. sparse autoencoder toy-model setup, but focuses on permutation-symmetric data and the large-input-dimension regime, analyzing weight statistics and reconstruction loss rather than measuring individual-neuron feature mixtures.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper studies changes in sparsity p, compression ratio nd/ns, and input dimension ns; it reports that statistical symmetry improves as ns grows.

fits_no_version.finding: In permutation-symmetric toy autoencoders, loss is O(p) as r→0 and about p²/r (up to log factors) at high sparsity. Any elementwise or filtering decoder faces the same lower bound.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In toy sparse autoencoders, elementwise or selection decoders can improve reconstruction only by a constant factor over ReLU.

fits_no_version.finding: An artificial weight construction with only large-scale symmetric statistics matches trained-model loss.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Trained toy superposition models rely on large-scale weight statistics, not microscopic weight structure.

record.problems: The paper studies a restricted permutation-symmetric toy-model regime, not vision or language-model neurons. The text gives inconsistent conditions for one high-sparsity loss scaling. Reconstruction-loss results do not establish how often individual neurons have unrelated meanings.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-version results were omitted. Results on weight-statistic fluctuations and Gaussianity were not extracted as claim findings because they do not measure individual-neuron polysemanticity or its proposed causes.

untested.parts: No vision models or neuron input responses.
Superposition is assumed as framing; whether superposition causes neurons to respond to unrelated features is not measured.
No study of polysemanticity arising without capacity pressure.
Activation-function variants are discussed only for reconstruction loss, not for polysemantic-neuron share.

record.verdict_notes: This is a theory and toy-model paper on superposition decoding, with no neuron-level polysemanticity data. Fig. 3 weight statistics (diagonals 1.29±.01, bias −.18±.01) concern feature routing, not neuron meanings, and were correctly left out.

versions.untested_parts: No vision classifier neurons or their input responses are examined.
No language-model MLP neurons, tokens, or contexts are examined.
The paper studies a bottlenecked sparse autoencoder toy model, but does not measure whether individual neurons pack unrelated features or test that as the cause of polysemanticity.
No initialization, regularization, or training-noise effects on neuron polysemanticity are tested.
The paper discusses decoder architecture and reconstruction performance, but does not measure polysemantic-neuron shares or changes in those shares.
No neuron explanations or shared-feature interpretations are assessed.
The paper does not compare neuron-polysemanticity measurements across activation ranges or explanation-scoring methods.

rows.subject: trained toy models (aggregate)
rows.size_stated: input dimension ns varied; examples include ns = 128, 512, and 8192
rows.operation_detail: Measured reconstruction loss as a function of compression ratio and sparsity.

conditions.value: permutation-symmetric sparse inputs; xi = ci ui, with ci ~ Bernoulli(p) and ui ~ Uniform[0, 1]

rows.value: The text reports loss of O(p) as r approaches 0 and derives a high-sparsity scaling of O(p²/r) up to logarithmic factors; its discussion gives inconsistent conditions for the latter scaling.
rows.note: This is a reconstruction-loss result for the toy model, not a measurement of individual neurons' feature mixtures. The text's statements about the condition for O(p²/r) are inconsistent.
rows.check: Toy-model reconstruction-loss result, not a polysemanticity measure; linking to none is correct. The summary in Section 5.1 states the condition 'pr ≪ 1' for both scalings, an evident typo the record correctly flags.

rows.subject: trained toy models (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared trained-model reconstruction loss with that of an optimized artificial Persian-rug weight construction.
rows.value: The losses are described as essentially the same; the paper says the Persian-rug model's loss matches trained-model loss closely.
rows.note: Aggregate comparison as described by the authors; no numerical values are stated in the text.
rows.check: Compares the authors' forward-engineered construction with trained models (method validation). This is not a claim finding; it is correctly unlinked.

rows.subject: general elementwise or selection-type decoder
rows.operation_detail: Derived a lower bound on reconstruction loss for decoders that act elementwise or filter elements.

conditions.value: sparse inputs with active values uniform on [0, 1]

rows.value: The text derives a lower bound of order p²/r, up to logarithmic corrections, for the stated decoder class.
rows.note: A theoretical result about toy-model decoding performance, not about neuron polysemanticity.
rows.check: Analytic lower bound (Appendix D) on decoder loss, not an empirical measure of neuron behaviour; linking to none is correct.
